title: Monitoring Dissolved Oxygen
text: BREATHE is a 3 year (2025-2028) Water4All project developing innovative, sensor-based approaches to monitor river health and ecosystem services. By using continuous dissolved oxygen measurements and river metabolism indicators, the project aims to provide a new generation of tools for assessing ecosystem functioning, supporting sustainable water management, and informing environmental policy.

title: Monitoring Dissolved Oxygen
text:
Background
Current indicators used in national river health assessment systems (e.g. EU Water Framework Directive) do not reflect well biodiversity, aquatic ecosystem functioning and services as needed for new and proposed policies. Progress in sensor technology over the last 20 years has allowed the continuous monitoring of dissolved oxygen and river metabolism (photosynthesis, respiration, metabolic balance) at unprecedented spatio-temporal scale and resolution.
BREATHE’s main objective is to co-design an international sensor-based River Observation System (RIOS) including dissolved oxygen and whole river metabolism to quantify aquatic ecosystem services such as climate regulation, water purification, provisioning fisheries for the implementation of European and global policies (EU 2030 Biodiversity Strategy, European Green Deal net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, United Nations Sustainable Development Goals – notably Water and Sanitation for all.
BREATHE will reach this goal by engaging with stakeholders to: first, co-design a workflow from data collection to storage, integration and modelling, and second, co-construct case studies to demonstrate how the workflow may be applied at the local scale and integrated internationally.
The case studies are including key environmental issues in six countries:

Forest restoration (Brazil)
Water scarcity (Spain)
Multiple stressors (Switzerland)
Urban anoxia (United Kingdom)
Water regulation (Norway)
Climate change impacts (Sweden)

BREATHE will not only identify commonalities among regions, sharing solutions to barriers of implementation, but also focus on region-specific needs in aquatic ecosystem services and policies. Patterns, processes and experiences from low latitude might become future scenarios for higher latitudes.
BREATHE will provide guidance documents to optimise the development of monitoring networks, harmonise data collection and integration, and the modelling of the effect of drivers or remediation actions (restoration) on river ecosystem services.

title: Modeling
text:
Create test datasetCalculate NPP & GPP



# Create a sequence of datetime values at 1-hour intervals for four consecutive days
datetimes <- seq(
  from = as.POSIXct("2025-05-01 00:00:00"),
  to = as.POSIXct("2025-05-04 23:00:00"),
  by = "hour"
)

# Create light (PAR) daily pattern (24 values)
daily_pattern <- c(
  0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 20, 100, 300, 600, 900, 1300, 1500,
  1500, 1300, 900, 600, 300, 100, 20, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0
)

# Repeat the pattern for each day (4 days)
PAR_values <- rep(daily_pattern, times = 4)

# Join datetimes and PAR_values into a dataframe
df <- data.frame(
  DateTime = datetimes,
  PAR = PAR_values
)




# Assume GPP is related to PAR with a Michaelis Menten type equation
# The parameters are:

kPAR=500
GPPmax=2

df <- data.frame(
  DateTime = datetimes,
  PAR = PAR_values
) %>%
  mutate(GPP = GPPmax*PAR/(kPAR+PAR))

# Assume ER constant -0.54 
ER = -0.54

df <- df %>%
  mutate(ER = ER)

# calculate NEP = GPP + ER (ER negative number, as ER consumes O2)
df <- df %>%
  mutate(NEP = GPP+ER)







Carbon and oxygen concentrations over timePlotting



# assume normal atmospheric pressure (760 mm Hg = 1013 mbar or hPa) and
# constant temperature at 20°C, so oxygen saturation concentration is
# Cs=9.59 g O2 m-3 or mg O2 L-1.

Cs = 9.59

# Assume gas transfer velocity equivalent to gas exchange coefficient (h-1)
# with depth = 1m

k = 0.1 

# Now calculated changes in C, oxygen concentration over time
# seed value C0 for the first row

C0 = 9.0

# Create new column for C with NA values
df$Ct <- NA
# set first row equal the seed value
df$Ct[1] <- C0

# Loop through rows to calculate C recursively
for (i in 2:nrow(df)) {
  df$Ct[i] <- (k * Cs + df$NEP[i] + df$C[i - 1]) / (1 + k)
}


# Calculate flux of O2 at the water - air interface

df <- df %>%
  mutate(F = k*(Cs-Ct))

# View the first few rows
head(df)

# Plot C
ggplot(df, aes(x = DateTime, y = Ct)) +
  geom_line(size=1.5) + 
  labs(x = "Time",
       y = "Ct") +
  theme_minimal()




library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# Constants
Cs <- 9.59
ER <- -0.54
GPPmax <- 2
kPAR <- 500
C0 <- 9.0
k_values <- c(0.1, 0.5, 1, 5)

# Create datetime and PAR
datetimes <- seq(
  from = as.POSIXct("2025-05-01 00:00:00", tz = "UTC"),
  to = as.POSIXct("2025-05-04 23:00:00", tz = "UTC"),
  by = "hour"
)

daily_pattern <- c(
  0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 20, 100, 300, 600, 900, 1300, 1500,
  1500, 1300, 900, 600, 300, 100, 20, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0
)

PAR_values <- rep(daily_pattern, times = 4)

# Base dataframe
base_df <- data.frame(
  DateTime = datetimes,
  PAR = PAR_values
) %>%
  mutate(
    GPP = GPPmax * PAR / (kPAR + PAR),
    ER = ER,
    NEP = GPP + ER
  )

# Function to compute Ct for a given k
compute_Ct <- function(df, k, C0, Cs) {
  Ct <- numeric(nrow(df))
  Ct[1] <- C0
  for (i in 2:nrow(df)) {
    Ct[i] <- (k * Cs + df$NEP[i] + Ct[i - 1]) / (1 + k)
  }
  return(Ct)
}

# Create a long-format dataframe with Ct for each k
df_all <- bind_rows(
  lapply(k_values, function(k) {
    df_k <- base_df
    df_k$Ct <- compute_Ct(df_k, k, C0, Cs)
    df_k$k <- as.factor(k)
    df_k
  })
)

# Plot
ggplot(df_all, aes(x = DateTime, y = Ct, color = k)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Ct over Time for Different k Values",
    y = "Ct (Oxygen Concentration)",
    color = "k value"
  ) 
# note influence of initial value at start of first day
# plot without first day, two days are enough
ggplot(df_all, aes(x = DateTime, y = Ct, color = k)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Ct over Time for Different k Values",
    y = "Ct (Oxygen Concentration)",
    color = "k value"
  ) +
scale_x_datetime(
  limits = as.POSIXct(c("2025-05-02", "2025-05-04")),
  date_breaks = "1 day",
  date_labels = "%d %b"
) 

# What do you observe ?

title: Sweden
text:
The Arctic is warming twice as fast as the rest of the planet, driving rapid environmental change across the region. While changes in arctic terrestrial ecosystems are well documented through satellite imagery, the impacts of climate change on Arctic river ecosystems remain less understood. Assessing these impacts requires in-situ sensors to capture changes in river ecosystem processes over time and identify the environmental factors driving these changes.
To investigate how Arctic rivers respond to a changing climate, we established monitoring sites across a climate gradient spanning boreal forest, birch forest, and tundra-dominated rivers. These distinct vegetation zones are expected to shift in distribution and composition as temperatures rise. By monitoring river ecosystem processes across this gradient, we aim to identify how vegetation and associated environmental conditions shape river functioning. This approach will help us understand how Arctic rivers may respond to ongoing environmental change and improve predictions of their future responses to a warming climate.

title: Switzerland
text:
Switzerland Case Study
We focus on rivers exposed to multiple stressors: from climate driven hydrological shifts typical of glacier-fed catchments, to agricultural, anthropic and land use pressures in the downstream environments. Switzerland’s case studies provide a critical testbed for evaluating how river functioning responds to these combined impacts along the river continuum, and how sensor- based monitoring can support more resilient water management strategies. Our interest is to explore similarities and differences among metabolic cycles, and how each system responds to hydrological and biogeochemical stressors. 

Saxon agricultural ditch 

RQ: How do groundwater supply, agricultural inputs, and water-level regulation interact to control metabolism and CO₂ emissions in an agricultural drainage channel? 
The sensor station is located within an agricultural ditch originally dredged as part of a channel network designed to drain groundwater from the Rhône Valley and now primarily used for irrigation. Groundwater is thus the dominant water source, but the channel also receives urban and agricultural runoff. Consequently, the channel is generally characterized by low dissolved oxygen concentrations and high CO₂ levels. Hypoxic conditions, defined here as dissolved oxygen concentrations below 5 mg L⁻¹, occasionally occur during winter. In spring, however, the development of a well-established macrophyte community enhances photosynthetic oxygen production, raising dissolved oxygen concentrations to approximately 10 mg L⁻¹. 
SENSOR PARAMETERS: O2, CO2, turbidity, CDOM, water depth, temperature, conductivity 
WEEKLY GRAB SAMPLING: stable isotopes, DIC, DOC, nutrients, ions 

Martigny urban river 

RQ: How do urban carbon inputs and upstream flow regulation control metabolism and CO2 emissions in an urban river? 
We are monitoring the Drance river downstream Martigny urban area, just before its entrance in the Rhône. Our station is located at the closure of a 700 km2 river basin, with average annual discharge around 10 m3/s. At this site, we expect ecosystem functioning to reflect the combined effects of anthropogenic pollution and flow alteration, as the upstream catchment is influenced by multiple dams and water-intake structures. These effects may also interact with glacier-driven hydrological dynamics, given that approximately 10% of the catchment is glacierized. 
SENSOR PARAMETERS: O2, CO2, turbidity, CDOM, water depth, temperature, conductivity 
WEEKLY GRAB SAMPLING: stable isotopes, DIC, DOC, nutrients, ions 

Valsorey glacier-fed stream network 

RQ: How do glacier type and proglacial landscape configuration regulate the spatial propagation of metabolic activity through a high-alpine stream network? 
The first study site is the Valsorey glacier-fed stream network, that drains a high-altitude catchment, in which approximately 20% of the area is dominated by ice dynamics. This network originates from different glacier sources, i.e. clean ice glaciers and talus/rock glaciers, that control flow and turbidity dynamics across the year. Reaches fed by different types of glaciers strongly differ in turbidity and hydrologic deliveries, both in timing and magnitude. We currently monitor 11 sites spanning glacier floodplains and the catchment output, to assess how hydrologic variability and carbon delivery influence ecosystem functioning at different altitudes.  
SENSOR PARAMETERS: O2, turbidity, CDOM, water depth, temperature, conductivity 
WEEKLY GRAB SAMPLING: stable isotopes, DIC, DOC, nutrients, ions 
Overall RQ: How do hydrological and land-use shifts govern the transition of streams from passive carbon conveyors to metabolically active reactors across glacier-fed, urban dominated, and groundwater-fed agricultural ecosystems?

title: Spain
text:
La Tordera is 52 km long stream that drains 898 km². It is located between the Catalan coastal and pre-coastal mountain ranges, draining into the Mediterranean Sea. It collects water from the northern slopes of the Montnegre massif and the southern slopes of Montseny, both part of the protected natural parks network and Natura 2000 network. The basin’s geology is complex but mainly consists of siliceous materials (granite, schist, and gneiss) resulting in predominantly sandy soils. The region covers a widely altitudinal gradient (from 0 to 1700 m a.s.l.), and the orography is particularly pronounced on the Montseny side, where the altitude rises from 100 m a.s.l. to 1700 m a.s.l. in just 10 km of horizontal line. The climate is typically Mediterranean, with hot, dry summers and mild winters, but the marked orography provides diverse microclimates ranging from semi-arid Mediterranean at lower altitudes (100-1000 m a.s.l.) to humid temperate and cool sub-alpine climates at higher altitudes (1000-1700 m a.s.l.).
Average annual rainfall varies between 600 and 1100 mm and usually falls during spring and autumn, with occasional summer storms. The headwaters are mainly forested and primarily covered by sclerophyllous forests. At higher altitudes, there are deciduous beech forests. In general, headwater streams of La Tordera have a well-developed riparian forest (10-15-m wide). In the lowland valleys, the long tradition of human settlements has created a very heterogeneous mosaic of land uses, where forests have been partially replaced by agricultural, urban and industrial areas.The geological and climatic diversity of the area shapes the hydrological regimes of La Tordera’s tributaries, ranging from permanent streams in humid zones to intermittent ones in semi-arid Mediterranean areas.
In the BREATHE Spain project, we will install 10 monitoring stations across the Tordera River basin, located at five headwater sites (La Llavina, Santa Fe, Font del Regàs, Castanyet, and Fuirosos) and five sites along the main channel (Santa Maria de Palautordera, Sant Celoni, Fuirosos Tributary, Arbúcies Tributary, and Fogars). Each station will be equipped with high-frequency sensors (recording data every 10 minutes) measuring dissolved oxygen, temperature, electrical conductivity, water level, and solar radiation. These stations will help us understand how oxygen dynamics vary across the landscape in response to hydrological and physicochemical conditions.
